newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean sugar firms deny Hong Kong export delays.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean sugar firms deny Hong Kong export delays.

text.p: South Korea's three sugar refiners denied on Monday that any of their plants were on strike and said there were no delays in shipments to Hong Kong as reported by traders in the British colony.
"We haven't heard of any strike at our plant so far," said an official with Cheiljedang Corp.

Spokesmen for Taihan Sugar Corp and Sam Yang Co Ltd also said their plants had not been been hit by nationwide industrial stoppages in protest at a new labour law passed by the National Assembly last Thursday.
Of the three, only Taihan Sugar has a labour union, but union officials at the company could not immediately be reached for comment.
Earlier, traders in Hong Kong told Reuters that South Korean sugar exports had been delayed by a few days due to a strike at one refiner's plant.
South Korea supplies between 7,000-8,000 tonnes of sugar a month to Hong Kong -- about 70 percent of the colony's total imports, they added.

The traders said the tolling of sugar in China for Hong Kong would probably increase to between 1,500-2,000 tonnes a month, from about 1,000 tonnes now, over the next few weeks to cover the anticipated supply shortfall.

The South Korean sugar refiners said that while they had been unaffected by the country's industrial unrest so far, they were concerned this could change if the strikes spread to transport and major ports.

"If the strike hits South Korea's major ports and transportation industry, there may be some impact on exports," the Cheiljedang spokesman said. "But so far we haven't heard anything on that," he added.

The Korea Sugar Manufacturers Association said the three refiners produced 1.13 million tonnes of sugar in 1995 (Cheiljedang Corp, 507,000 tonnes, Taihan Sugar 297,000 tonnes, and Sam Yang 328,000 tonnes) and exported 240,000 tonnes.
An association official said about 40 percent of total sugar exports went to Hong Kong last year.
